title: Watts and Wesley
hook: two Englishmen wrote thousands of hymns still sung, like When I Survey and And Can It Be

segments.voice: Yesterday: the church sings, psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, from the upper room to a prison cell at midnight. Your line was who sings prays twice. Did one line of a song escape you? Day one hundred thirty-six.

An English chapel, and a teenager named Isaac Watts sits in the pews, bored. The churches he knew sang mainly the psalms, set into stiff rhymes, often lined out one line at a time by a leader and dragged back by the congregation. The story goes that young Isaac complained, and his father said, more or less: then write something better. So he did. Not one hymn. Hymn after hymn. Some are still sung at Christmas and on Good Friday. A generation later, a restless Anglican priest named Charles Wesley would write thousands more. Between them, these two men gave English-speaking congregations a new kind of song. Today's word is what they wrote.
screen: `A BORED TEENAGER IN CHURCH.` → `THEN WRITE SOMETHING BETTER.` → `HYMN AFTER HYMN.`

segments.voice: Hymn. From the Greek hymnos, a song of praise to a god or a hero. For Christians, a hymn is a song of praise written in verses, sung by the whole congregation. Isaac Watts did something that sounds simple now and was daring then. He wrote new songs in plain English, in the voice of the people singing them, about the gospel. People call him the father of English hymnody. He wrote Joy to the World. He wrote O God, Our Help in Ages Past. And he wrote When I Survey the Wondrous Cross, published in 1707. It walks slowly toward the cross, looks, and ends with a line that turned into today's carry: "Love so amazing, so divine, Demands my soul, my life, my all." Read it again as a poem, and notice it doesn't argue. It just looks and answers. Then Charles Wesley. He and his brother John started the movement that became the Methodists, and Charles wrote hymns by the thousand. Hark! the Herald Angels Sing. Love Divine, All Loves Excelling. And And Can It Be, written around the time of his own conversion in 1738. It is full of astonishment: "Amazing love! How can it be That Thou, my God, shouldst die for me?" One man a careful poet, the other a fountain. Watts was a Congregationalist; Wesley an Anglican. Their hymns now turn up in the hymnals of churches neither man belonged to. Both keep landing on the same astonished word: amazing. A hymn is theology you can sing, in words plain enough that a tired congregation can carry it home.
screen: `HYMNOS — A SONG OF PRAISE.` · `WATTS: WHEN I SURVEY, 1707.` · `WESLEY: HYMNS BY THE THOUSAND.` · `THEOLOGY YOU CAN SING.` · then, large: `LOVE SO AMAZING, SO DIVINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a hymn verse as a poem. Take the last verse of When I Survey. Say it slowly, not sung, just spoken, with a pause at every comma. "Were the whole realm of nature mine, That were a present far too small; Love so amazing, so divine, Demands my soul, my life, my all." Now sit with it. Which word catches? Realm. Small. Demands. Let it catch. If you pray, you can pray it back slowly. If you don't, just read it as what it is: a man looking at something and finding his hands empty. The bell holds the time.
Hymn. From the Greek hymnos, a song of praise. A poem in verses, made for a whole congregation to sing.
Your line: love so amazing. Today, look up one hymn by Watts or Wesley and read a single verse slowly, like a poem. Day one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Many churches sing hymns by Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley from printed hymnals or screens, especially at Christmas, Easter and funerals, and some Christians read hymns privately as poems or prayers.

myth: Watts and Wesley belonged to the same church
Watts was a Congregationalist; Charles Wesley was an Anglican priest. their hymns crossed church lines anyway.
Charles Wesley wrote only a handful of hymns
he wrote thousands, including Hark! the Herald Angels Sing and And Can It Be.
Watts and Wesley are only sung by Methodists

fork.setup: you're a teenager in church, bored by the singing, and you complain. your father says: then write something better. what do you do?
options: shrug it off and keep complaining.
write a new hymn for the next Sunday.
fork.reveal: the story goes that young Isaac Watts did exactly that, and kept going, hymn after hymn. the story is told often; the details are hard to confirm.

original.note: Greek: a song of praise, sung to a god or a hero. the English word hymn comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn is any old church song.
what it means: a poem of praise in verses, written for a whole congregation to sing, theology plain enough to carry home.
what a scholar hears: in England, singing new hymns rather than only metrical psalms was once controversial. Watts helped change that, and Wesley's hymns carried the Methodist revival.

notes: The Watts origin story (complaining about the singing, his father's challenge) is traditional and hard to verify; the script says 'the story goes'. Confirm.
Charles Wesley's output: commonly given as about 6,000 (some say more, up to around 9,000 poems). Script says 'somewhere around six thousand'. Confirm.

Watts: 'father of English hymnody' is a common title. Watts was a Congregationalist (Independent) minister; confirm. Joy to the World (1719, from Psalm 98) and O God, Our Help in Ages Past (Psalm 90) are his. Confirm.
And Can It Be: usually dated to 1738, around Charles Wesley's conversion (May 1738). Confirm.

Hymn texts quoted from the original 18th-century texts; verify punctuation and wording against a standard early edition (e.g. 1707/1709 Hymns and Spiritual Songs has 'Were the whole realm of nature mine').
Lining out: the practice of a leader reading or singing one line for the congregation to repeat. Confirm description.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'around three hundred years ago', 'most English churches', 'hundreds', 'every Christmas', the superlative 'the finest hymn in English', 'verse almost every day' and 'six thousand' (now 'thousands', as the index says), and the list of denominations that sing them. The myth about 'most English churches' is replaced with Watts's and Wesley's different churches.
